Level 2 · Intermediate · Week 11

Project Studio 2

Tests check the brain of your program, playtesters check the fun, and polish makes it work for everyone.

What you will learn

  • How to add data to your project: a list, a dictionary and a file that saves and loads (Milestone M3).
  • How to write at least three pytest tests for your own functions.
  • How to run a playtest and turn feedback into a bug list.
  • How to check your project for accessibility, then polish it (Milestone M4).

The big idea: test the brain, playtest the fun

Your program has two kinds of functions. Logic functions (the brain) take values in and give an answer back with return: pytest can check those automatically. Drawing functions (the paint) make pictures: a computer cannot tell whether your star looks nice, but a playtester can.

Two tricks make your functions easy to test:

  1. Put the start-up code (make the screen, start the loop) under if __name__ == "__main__":. Then pytest can borrow your functions without starting the game.

  2. Give file functions the file name as a parameter. Then the game and the tests can use different files, for example highscore.txt for playing and test_scores.txt for testing, and your tests never wipe your real high score.

Test a normal case (an everyday value) and edge cases (values at the very limit: the edge of the screen, a score of 0, a file that does not exist yet). Bugs love to hide at the edges.

Your project needs all three. Write where each one lives in your code.

Data Its name in my code What it remembers

Exercise11.2: Write three tests

Plan your tests first. Pick functions that return something.

Function Input Expected answer Normal or edge?
next_x 280, 1 280 (stays on screen) edge

Make a new file in the same folder as your game. Its name must start with test_, for example test_mygame.py. Each test is a function whose name starts with test_:

test\_mygame.py (part)

from mygame import load_high_score, next_x, save_high_score

def test_stops_at_the_right_edge():
    assert next_x(280, 1) == 280

def test_high_score_round_trip():
    save_high_score(42, "test_scores.txt")
    assert load_high_score("test_scores.txt") == 42

To run them: press F5 on your game once, close its window, then in Thonny choose Tools > Open system shell… and type (use python3 if python is not found):

python -m pytest test_mygame.py -v

PASSED means the function gave the expected answer. FAILED means it did not: read the line starting with E to see what came out instead. A test that fails is not a disaster, it is a bug you found before a player did!

Exercise11.3: Playtest with feedback cards

Swap computers with another team (or ask a family member) and play their project for 4 minutes. Fill in a card for them. Be kind and specific.

I liked…

I was confused when…

A bug I saw (what I did / what happened / what I expected):

One idea…

Back at your own project, turn the cards into a bug list. Mark each line MUST (it crashes or you cannot play), SHOULD (it is confusing) or COULD (a nice idea). Fix the MUST lines first.

What I did What happened What I expected MUST / SHOULD / COULD

Exercise11.4: Accessibility review and polish (M4)

Make your project work for as many people as possible. Check off each line or fix it.

One change I made:

Reflect

Which test are you proudest of? What bug did it catch, or could it catch?

What did a playtester notice that you had not noticed?

New words

playtest
letting someone else use your program while you watch and take notes.
normal case
a test with an everyday value, like moving from the middle of the screen.
edge case
a test with a value at the very limit, like the edge of the screen, zero, or a missing file.
accessibility
designing so that everyone can use it, including people who see colors differently or read more slowly.
polish
small finishing touches that make a working program clearer and nicer to use.
bug list
a list of problems found in testing, sorted so the most important ones get fixed first.

Homework: Project Studio 2

15–20 minutes. Do Core first; Challenge and Creative are optional.

CoreThree passing tests and one fix (about 10 minutes)

  1. Open your project folder in Thonny. Make sure you have a file called test_mygame.py (or test_ plus your game’s name) with at least 3 tests.

  2. Run your game once with F5, close its window, then Tools > Open system shell… and type python -m pytest -v (or python3 -m pytest -v).

  3. Copy the last line of the output here (for example “3 passed in 0.05s”):

  4. Pick the top MUST line from your playtest bug list and fix it. What did you fix?

ChallengeTest first

Find a bug or a missing feature in a logic function. Write the test first and run it: it should say FAILED. Then change your code until it says PASSED. Write your test here:

Why is it useful to see the test fail first?

CreativeHow to play

Add a “how to play” message to your project’s screen (with write and a font size of 18 or more), or write it on a card to place next to the computer at the showcase. Include: the goal, the keys, and how the game ends (or, for an Art Studio, how to draw, save and load). Test it on a family member: can they start without asking you anything?

Self-checkSelf-check: tick each box when it is true
